N.K. Saha, Senior Advocate, instructed by Gias Uddin Ahmed, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioner (in all the cases)

full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah J. These five criminal petitions for leave to appeal have been filed by the accused against the judgment and order dated the 13th day of April, 2016 passed a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 46461 of 2015 heard and disposed of analogously with Criminal Miscellaneous Case Nos. 46462, 46463, 46464 and 46465 all of 2015 discharging all the Rules issued in the respective miscellaneous case with costs. 

 2. The above mentioned criminal miscellaneous cases were filed before the High Court Division by the accused petitioner for quashing the criminal proceedings vide Sessions Case No. 178 of 2015 arising out of Complaint Register (C.R) Case No.1853 of 2014 (Kotwali Zone), Sessions Case No. 175 of 2015 arising out of C.R. Case No. 1851 of 2014 (Kotwali Zone), Sessions Case No. 177 of 2015 arising out of C.R. Case No. 1852 of 2014 (Kotawali Zone), Sessions Case No. 176 of 2015 arising out of C.R. Case No. 1850 of 2014 (Kotwali Zone) and Sessions Case No. 174 of 2015 arising out of C.R. Case No. 1854 of 2014 (Kotwali Zone). All the C.R. cases were filed under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, in short, the Act, 1881 now pending before the Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong. In all the cases, the same complainant alleged that the accused different chaques of different amount in his favour. The cheques were placed before the concerned Bank for encashment and all the cheques except one were dishonoured by the Bank for 'stop payment' instructing given to the Bank by the accused. The other one was dishonoured for insufficiency of fund. Therefore, the complainant had filed five separate complaint petitions under section 138(1) of the Act, 1881 after compliance with the procedures laid down in the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 138 thereof giving rise to the above mentioned respective C.R. case. The cases being triable by a Court of Section, the records were transmitted to the Court of Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Chittagong and were registered as the respective Sessions case in the number mentioned above. The respective Sessions case was transferred to the Court of Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong for trial, who framed charge in the respective case against the accused under section 138 of the Act, 1881 by rejecting the petition filed by him under section 265C of the Code of Criminal Procedure (the Code). Then the accused filed five separate applications under section 561A of the Code before the High Court Division quashing the respective Sessions case as stated earlier and obtained the respective Rule. A Division Bench by the impugned judgment and order discharged the Rules with costs; hence these petitions for leave to appeal. 

 3. Heard Mr. N.K. Saha, learned Advocate for the petitioner in all the petitions and Mr. Helal Uddin Mollah, learned Advocate who entered caveat on behalf of complainant-respondent No.2, perused the respective petition for complaint, the order of the learned Advocate who entered caveat on behalf of complainant-respondent No.2, perused the respective petition of complaint, the order of the learned Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge framing charge against the accused in the respective Sessions case and the impugned judgment and order. 

 4. So far as the decision of the High Court Division in refusing to quash the proceedings of the respective Sessions case is concerned, we find no legal infirmity therein. In the petition of complaint, a clear prima-facie case having been made out, the learned Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge rightly framed charge against the accused in the respective Sessions case. Therefore, we find nothing to interfere with the decision of the High Court Division as to the merit of the respective application for quashing made before it. But we need to decide a very important question whether the High Court Division could award costs against the accused for taka 10,000.00 in each case and though in 5(five) cases, the total amount of costs would come to taka 50,000.00 and then could it in specific term direct the accused to pay taka 1,00,000.00 (one lac). 

 5. In awarding the costs, the reasons assigned by the High Court Division, inter alia, are that in a case under the Act, 1881, costs may be awarded to the aggrieved party for causing financial hardship, leading a person or a family to the verge of ruination, for harassment and the inflicting mental agony on frivolous grounds or by resorting to dilatory tactics or on issues of law already settled by the Appellate Division, i.e. where the accused petitioner does not come in clean heads for seeking justice, but with collateral purpose; a case filed under section 138(1) of the Act, 1881, is unlike any other criminal case, in that, here the proceeding starts upon a complaint petition filed by an aggrieved person, i.e. the payee, not at the instance of the 'State'; the State is not a 'necessary' party though it may be 'proper' party in case under the Act, 1881; the cheque bears the proprietary and pecuniary interest of the payee and the law provides for realization of fine to be paid to the payee, vide sub-section (2) of section 138; by way of amendment, done by Act No. III of 2006 (09.02.2006), section 138A has been inserted making provisions to deposit not less than 50% of the amount of the dishonored cheque, in the trial Court, as a pre-condition to prefer appeal; there is no similar provision for preferring appeal by a person convicted under any other law; apparently, the Act, 1881 is a piece of beneficial legislation and distinct from other penal law; hence, in appropriate case, costs may be awarded in case under the Act, 1881. 

 6. The Rule was contested by the complainant-opposite party by filing a counter affidavit and nowhere in the counter affidavit, any case of his being on the "verge of ruination, for harassment and for inflicting mental agony on frivolous grounds or by resorting the dilatory tactics or on issues of law already settled by the Appellate Division, i.e. when the accused-petitioner does not come in clean hands for seeking justice, but with collateral purpose and/or for causing financial hardship to the complaint" were made out. 

 9. So far as the Ct, 1881 is concerned, there is no provision therein authorizing a criminal Court trying an offence under section 138 of the Act, 1881 or the High Court Division in any proceeding arising out of any case in connection with a case under the said Act to award costs either to the accused or to the complainant. 

 10. So far as the Code is concerned except section 148(3), there is no express provision for awarding cost. And section 148(3) is altogether a different provision and it relates to a dispute as to immovable property and this kind of dispute is dealt with by the executive Magistrate. Section 544, 545 and 546A of the Code, however, allow a criminal Court to pass an order to pay compensation to the complainant for defraying the expenses of prosecution. Section 250 of the Code also authorizes a criminal Court to pay compensation to the accused for filing false or frivolous case. However, section 344 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides for adjournment "On such terms" as the Court thinks fit, covers a direction to one of the parties to pay cost of the adjournment. In the case of Md. Habibur Rahman -V- State and another, 1981, DLR, 443 A.T.M Afzal, J (as then he was) sitting singly considering the provisions of the various section of the Code, such as, section 544, 545, 344 and 546A of the Code held: 

 12. The fact of the case (Md. Habibur Rahman) was the opposite party No.2 (in the High Court Division), Musammat Sufia Khatoon, instituted a criminal case under section 493 of the Penal Code against the petitioner in the Court of the Sub-Division Magistrate, Tangial on 7-2-1978. A warrant of arrest having been issued, the petitioner appeared before the Sub-Division Magistrate and obtained bail in due course. The case was then transferred to the Court of Mr. Fazulur Rahman Bhuiyan, Magistrate, obviously for the purpose of holding and enquiry under Chapter XVIII of the Code. The case was fixed for hearing on 11-8-1979. On that date, the petitioner remained absent from Court upon producing a medical certificate. The complainant, however, was present with 7(seven) witnesses of her. The Magistrate, by an order of the same date, observed that the witnesses stated that the petitioner had stated to attend the Court for taking time unnecessarily granted adjournment costs of taka 70.00. He further directed the petitioner to deposit the said costs on 24.8.1978 which was fixed as the next date for examining the witnesses. The Magistrate also observed that if the petitioner remained absent on the next date of hearing upon giving excuse, war-rant of arrest would be issued against him. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order of the Magistrate awarding adjournment costs, the petitioner moved the learned Sessions Judge in revision and the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Tangail, who heard the matter, dismissed the motion by the order dated 28.03.1979. Thereafter, the petitioner moved the High Court Division and obtained the Rule. 

 14. Section 344 of the Code is exercised during trial of a case and in the event as observed by A.T.M Afzal, J. a criminal Court at the stage of inquiry or trial may award adjournment costs "with circumspection and care and only under circumstances which call for it in the interest of justice." But the question is whether the High Court Division in exercising its inherent power under section 561A of the Code can award cost to any of the party of the proceedings, particularly, the accused while discharging the Rule issued for quashing a criminal proceeding or not. As stated earlier in the Code, there is nothing to authorize the High Court Division or any criminal Court to award costs in a criminal case against the accused or the informant/complaint as the case may be. This question was precisely considered by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Mary Angel and others Vs. State of Tamil Nadu AIR 1999, S.0 2245. The Indian Supreme Court affirmed the order awarding costs by the High Court in exercise of its power under section 482 of the Code (our provision is 561 A of the Code) holding the "while exercising inherent jurisdiction under section 482, Court has power to pass 'such orders' (not inconsistent with any provision of the Code) including the order for costs in appropriate cases, (i) to give effect to any order passed under the Code or (ii) to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or (iii) otherwise to secure the ends of justice. As stated above, this extraordinary power is to be used in extraordinary circumstances and in a judicious manner. Costs may be to meet the litigation expenses or can be exemplary to achieve the aforesaid purpose." The facts of the case under which the Indian Supreme Court took the above quoted view were as under: 

 "3. FIR was lodged by Josephine Jaya on 29th September, 1989 stating that her in-laws demanded from her father Rs. 60,000/- in cash, 65 sovereigns of gold jewellery for the bride and nine sovereigns or similar jewellery for the groom; that out of Rs. 60,000/-, Rs. 50,000/- were paid, that after the marriage, she was treated cruelly and there were unlawful demands for a colour television and Rs. 50,000/- in cash. It is also alleged that at the instigation of in laws accused Nos. 2 to 6, accused No. 1 (her husband) administered certain medicine with a view to abort her pregnancy. After preliminary investigation on 18th October, 1989, a charge-sheet was filed against A-1 to A-6 under Section 498(A), 406, 420, 315 I.P.C. and Section 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act. The case was committed to the Sessions Court, Nagercoil and was numbered as Sessions Case No. 10 of 1989. Accused Nos. 3 to 6 filed an application under Section 227 of the Criminal Procedure Code for their discharge. That application was allowed by holding that they had not demanded dowry and there is no material to show that medicine for abortion was administered at their instigation. Against that order, complainant filed Criminal R.C. No. 442 of 1990 before the High Court of Madras, By Order dated 9th July, 1993, the High Court allowed the Revision case filed by the complainant and set aside the order of dis-charge. In pursuance of the said Order, on 13th June, 1996, learned Sessions Judge framed charges against accused Nos. 1-3 to 1-6 also. 

 4. Against that Order dated 13th June, 1996, accused Nos. 3 to 6, that is, the present appellants preferred Criminal Revision Case No. 601 of 1996 before the High Court on the ground that there was no prima facie case for framing of charges against them. The Court while dismissing the same observed that the proceedings have been dragged on for 8 years and that petition was filed without disclosing even to the learned Counsel that revision against the order of non-framing of charges was allowed earlier by the High Court by holding that there was sufficient material for framing charges. The Court also observed that despite the direction of the High Court to the Sessions Court to finish the trial as expeditiously as possible, appellants have not allowed the Sessions court to comply with the said directions of the High Court. Considering the aforesaid conduct, the High Court imposed costs of Rs. 10,000.00 each on the appellants to be paid to the informant (complaint) wife of accused No.1 and directed the sessions Court to dispose of the case. That order is challenged before us in this appeal." 

 15. From the facts of the above mentioned reported case, it is prima-facie clear that the accused in order to harass the informant resorted to various dilatory tactics and succeeded to drag the case for long 8(eight) year and that the application for quashing the proceedings was filed sup-pressing the fact even to their learned Counsel that earlier revision against the order of non-framing of charge was filed and the same was allowed by the High Court by holding that there was sufficient material for framing charge; despite the direction of the High Court to the Sessions Court to finish the trial as expeditiously as possible, the appellants did not allow the Sessions Court to comply with the said directions of the High Court and considering the aforesaid conduct of the accused, the High Court awarded costs of Rs. 10,000.00 each on the appellants to be paid to the informant, wife of accused No. 1 and directed the Sessions Court to dispose of the case within 2 (two) months from the date of communication of the order. 

 16. In our jurisdiction, ordinarily the High Court Division cannot exercise its inherent power in awarding costs. Over and above, there is no express provision in the Code authorizing the High Court Division to award costs in exercising its inherent power under section 561A of the code. The only provision in section 344 of the Code which authorizes a criminal Court to award costs during trial of a case. Other that section 344 of the Code, section 250, 544, 545, 546A of the Code empower a Court to pass an order to pay compensation only for defraying expenses of prosecution. 

 18. The facts and circumstances under which the Indian Supreme Court affirmed the order of the High Court in awarding costs against the accused may be example. In the facts and circumstances of the instant case, the High Court Division was not at all justified to award the costs against the accused inasmuch as no extraordinary circumstances existed in the instant case. In the instant case, after the charge was framed by the learned Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge, the accused-respondent moved the High Court Division under section 651 A of the Code and obtained the Rule which was discharged after final hearing. There is nothing on record that there was suppression of any fact or that due to the activities of the accused, the case was dragged. The reasons on which the High Court Division awarded the costs against the accused do not come within the preview of section 561A and moreso, no such case was made out by the complainant in counter affidavit. 

 20. For the discussions made above, we conclude that the High Court Division acted illegally and without jurisdiction in awarding costs of taka 10,000.00 in each case to the complainant while discharging the respective a Rule and them again directing the accused to pay a total costs of taka 1,00,000.00 (taka one lac) within 30 (thirty) days "of drawing upon" of the judgment and order of the Court. Therefore, that portion of the order of the High Court Division cannot be maintained and must be set aside and accordingly the words used in the ordering portion of the judgment to the effect "with cost. The accused petitioner is directed to pay cost of Tk. 10,000/- to the opposite No.1 in each case, in total Tk. 1,00,000/- (Taka one lac) within 30 days of drawing upon of this judgment and order of this court" are expunged.
